title: Dome 7: Running on Empty
hook: A greenhouse is flooded with light and surrounded by CO2, yet its plants have almost stopped making sugar. What could they possibly be short of?
briefing: Plants run on two linked machines. In the thylakoid membranes, light energy splits water and drives electrons down a chain, pumping hydrogen ions and producing ATP and NADPH. In the stroma, the Calvin cycle spends that ATP and NADPH so Rubisco can turn CO2 into sugar, and the whole system can only run as fast as its scarcest supply allows.
intro: Emergency lockdown. Dome 7's oxygen generator is offline and the greenhouse is now the only thing keeping the station breathable. A power surge sealed every subsystem behind a diagnostic lock. Restart the light reactor, then the carbon-fixation bay, then prove you know the dome's true output to unseal the airlock.
outro_win: The airlock hisses open. The greenhouse is back at full output, and you know exactly which supply to boost next.
outro_lose: The clock ran out with the greenhouse still sealed. Open the Field Guide, revisit the locks you missed, and try again.

checks.prompt: The sample cabinet will only open for the flask that was given heavy-oxygen WATER. Which flask was it?
hints: Re-read the Tracer lab notebook: compare the mass of the O2 each flask released.
Photosystem II splits water to replace the electrons it loses; ask which molecule's oxygen atoms end up in the O2 gas.
Similar case: if heavy-oxygen CO2 were the source of O2 gas, the flask fed heavy CO2 would release heavy O2 (mass 36). Apply the same logic to the real data.
options: Both flasks, because O2 comes from water and CO2 equally
Neither flask, because heavy oxygen would end up in the sugar

wrong_feedback.feedback: Flask B released ordinary O2 (mass 32). If you picked it, you may be assuming the O2 comes from CO2. Which molecule does Photosystem II split?

wrong_feedback.option: Both flasks, because O2 comes from water and CO2 equally
wrong_feedback.feedback: If both sources contributed, both flasks would show some heavy O2. Only one did. The oxygen in CO2 ends up in sugar and water, not O2 gas.

wrong_feedback.option: Neither flask, because heavy oxygen would end up in the sugar
wrong_feedback.feedback: That is true for CO2's oxygen, but one flask clearly released heavy O2 (mass 36). Where did that heavy oxygen come from?

checks.prompt: The ATP synthase housing will unlock when you enter how many times higher the H+ concentration is in the thylakoid lumen than in the stroma.
hints: Read the pH probe display: it gives the pH of the lumen and of the stroma.
Lower pH means more H+. Each 1-unit pH difference is a 10-fold difference in H+ concentration, and that stored gradient is what spins ATP synthase.
Similar example: a solution at pH 4 has 10 x 10 = 100 times more H+ than one at pH 6. Now apply it to the probe's two readings.

checks.prompt: The breaker panel asks you to confirm the DCMU leak before flushing bay 2. Which bay 2 reading proves it?
hints: Re-read the maintenance tag on the breaker panel: it says exactly which hand-off DCMU blocks.
Photosystem II keeps splitting water only as long as it can pass its electrons on down the chain. If that hand-off is blocked, what stops first?
Similar case: if a factory's exit conveyor jams, the machines feeding it soon stop too, even though power is still on. Which process feeds Photosystem II its electrons?
options: Light absorption drops to zero, because DCMU destroys chlorophyll
CO2 uptake stops but O2 release continues at full speed
No readings change, because Photosystem I can still absorb light
O2 release drops to zero, because water splitting has nowhere to send its electrons
answer: O2 release drops to zero, because water splitting has nowhere to send its electrons

wrong_feedback.option: Light absorption drops to zero, because DCMU destroys chlorophyll
wrong_feedback.feedback: The tag says DCMU blocks an electron hand-off; it doesn't touch the pigments. Chlorophyll still absorbs light, it just can't pass the energy on usefully.

wrong_feedback.option: CO2 uptake stops but O2 release continues at full speed
wrong_feedback.feedback: O2 comes from splitting water at Photosystem II, which needs somewhere to send its electrons. If PSII can't pass electrons on, can it keep splitting water?

wrong_feedback.option: No readings change, because Photosystem I can still absorb light
wrong_feedback.feedback: Photosystem I needs electrons delivered from Photosystem II in linear flow. Block the chain upstream and the whole line stalls.

checks.prompt: The export hatch opens only if you load exactly enough CO2 to export 5 G3P as sugar. How many CO2 molecules must enter the Calvin cycle?
hints: Use the Calvin cycle ledger: compare how many CO2 went in with how many G3P were exported.
Most G3P made by the cycle is recycled to rebuild RuBP; only the net G3P leaves as sugar. Each exported G3P holds 3 carbons, and every carbon came from one CO2.
Similar example: to export 2 G3P you need 2 x 3 = 6 CO2, just as the ledger shows. Scale that up.

checks.prompt: Before the vent will open, the controller asks for your diagnosis: why is sugar output falling even though the lights are on full?
hints: Read the Air-mix gauge: look at the O2 and CO2 levels and the state of the stomata.
Rubisco can bind O2 instead of CO2. When O2 is high and CO2 is low inside the leaf, it does this far more often, and that reaction wastes carbon and ATP.
Similar case: a cashier who grabs whatever coin is on top will grab the wrong coin more often when the wrong coins pile up. Which molecule is piling up in the dome?
options: The plants are using the extra O2 for cellular respiration and burning their sugar faster than they make it
Rubisco is grabbing O2 instead of CO2 (photorespiration), wasting carbon and ATP
The light reactions have stopped because there is not enough CO2 for them to split
The high O2 is bleaching the chlorophyll so it can no longer absorb light
answer: Rubisco is grabbing O2 instead of CO2 (photorespiration), wasting carbon and ATP

wrong_feedback.option: The plants are using the extra O2 for cellular respiration and burning their sugar faster than they make it
wrong_feedback.feedback: Cellular respiration isn't sped up by extra O2 like this. The gauge points to the enzyme that fixes carbon: what does Rubisco do when O2 is high and CO2 is low?

wrong_feedback.option: The high O2 is bleaching the chlorophyll so it can no longer absorb light
wrong_feedback.feedback: The gauge says the lights are fine and gives no sign of pigment damage. The problem is on the carbon-fixing side, not light absorption.

wrong_feedback.option: The light reactions have stopped because there is not enough CO2 for them to split
wrong_feedback.feedback: The light reactions split water, not CO2. CO2 is used by Rubisco in the Calvin cycle.

checks.prompt: Final lock. Use the fragments you collected: the ATP output, the NADPH output, and the cost of fixing one CO2. How many CO2 molecules per minute can the Calvin cycle actually fix?
hints: Look at your Fragments collected: you have the two supply rates and the cost of each CO2.
Work out how many CO2 each supply alone could pay for. A process can only run as fast as its scarcest input allows; the other supply is left over.
Similar example: a bakery with 20 eggs and 10 cups of flour, where each cake needs 2 eggs and 1 cup of flour, can make min(20/2, 10/1) = 10 cakes. Do the same with ATP and NADPH.

content.premise: You are the botanist on Mars research station Dome 7. The oxygen generator has failed, the greenhouse is locked down, and the station has twenty minutes of reserve air. Every greenhouse subsystem is sealed behind a diagnostic lock that only opens for someone who understands how the plants actually work.

rooms.name: Light Reactor Control Room
rooms.description: Rows of algae tanks glow under grow lamps. Warning lights blink over three sealed consoles: a sample cabinet, the ATP synthase housing, and the electron-flow breaker panel.

hotspots.label: Tracer lab notebook
hotspots.description: Experiment log, day 212: Two flasks of identical algae under the same light. One was given water made with heavy oxygen (18O); the other was given CO2 made with heavy oxygen. Everything else normal. Mass spectrometer on the released O2 gas: Flask A = mass 36 (both oxygen atoms heavy). Flask B = mass 32 (ordinary). The flask labels smeared in the surge.

hotspots.label: Sealed sample cabinet
hotspots.reveals_clue: Water supply: the O2 comes from split water, and the dome's water tank is full, so water is NOT a bottleneck.
hotspots.description: A cabinet holding the two unlabeled flasks. Its keypad reads: IDENTIFY THE HEAVY-WATER FLASK.

hotspots.label: pH probe display
hotspots.description: Two probes are inserted in a chloroplast sample. Thylakoid lumen: pH 5. Stroma: pH 8. Sticker on the display: each 1-unit drop in pH means 10 times more H+. ATP synthase only turns while H+ flows down its gradient.

hotspots.label: ATP synthase housing
hotspots.reveals_clue: ATP synthase restarted. Meter: ATP output = 21 per minute.
hotspots.description: A turbine-like model of ATP synthase, frozen mid-spin. The display reads: CONFIRM GRADIENT STRENGTH (fold difference in H+).

hotspots.label: Electron-flow breaker panel
hotspots.reveals_clue: Bay 2 flushed and electron flow restored. Meter: NADPH output = 16 per minute.
hotspots.description: Maintenance tag: "Weed-killer DCMU leaked into bay 2. DCMU stops plastoquinone from accepting electrons from Photosystem II." Bay 2 sensors: light absorption, O2 release, CO2 uptake.

rooms.name: Carbon Fixation Bay
rooms.description: Leafy racks fill a humid bay. The air tastes stale. An export hatch, a jammed air vent, and the airlock out of the dome are all sealed.

hotspots.label: Calvin cycle ledger
hotspots.description: Batch record: 6 CO2 entered the cycle and Rubisco attached each to RuBP. Consumed: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. Made: 12 G3P. Of those, 10 G3P were rebuilt into 6 RuBP and 2 G3P were exported as sugar.

hotspots.label: Sugar export hatch
hotspots.reveals_clue: Ledger footnote: every CO2 fixed costs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
hotspots.description: A hatch that feeds sugar to the station kitchen. Display: LOAD CO2 FOR 5 EXPORTED G3P.

hotspots.label: Air-mix gauge
hotspots.description: Dome air: O2 38%, CO2 0.01%. Leaf temperature: 35 C. Stomata: closed. Lights: full. Warning: sugar output falling.

hotspots.label: Air vent controller
hotspots.reveals_clue: Vent open: O2 back to 21% and CO2 restored. Photorespiration is now negligible, so count every Rubisco reaction as a CO2 fixed.
hotspots.description: A jammed vent between the bay and the station's air scrubber. The controller demands a diagnosis before it will open.

hotspots.label: Airlock
hotspots.description: The only way out. Its panel reads: ENTER TRUE CARBON-FIXATION RATE (CO2 per minute). Use the fragments you collected.

field_guide.title: Photolysis (water splitting)
field_guide.explanation: Photosystem II splits water to replace the electrons it loses. The oxygen atoms from water become the O2 gas plants release.

field_guide.title: Linear electron flow
field_guide.explanation: Electrons travel from Photosystem II through plastoquinone, the cytochrome complex and plastocyanin to Photosystem I, then to NADP+ to make NADPH. Blocking any hand-off stalls the whole line.

field_guide.title: Chemiosmosis in the chloroplast
field_guide.explanation: The electron chain pumps H+ into the thylakoid lumen. H+ flowing back out to the stroma through ATP synthase spins it and makes ATP.

field_guide.title: Calvin cycle
field_guide.explanation: In the stroma, Rubisco fixes CO2 onto RuBP; ATP and NADPH turn the product into G3P; most G3P rebuilds RuBP. Each CO2 fixed costs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, and 3 CO2 make one exported G3P.

field_guide.title: Rubisco and photorespiration
field_guide.explanation: Rubisco can grab O2 instead of CO2, especially when O2 is high, CO2 is low, and it's hot. That wastes carbon and ATP without making sugar.

field_guide.title: Limiting factors
field_guide.explanation: A process runs only as fast as its scarcest input. Real chloroplasts make slightly too little ATP by linear flow alone, so they top it up with cyclic electron flow.
